title.text: Language models: tokens, attention and next-word probability

objects.text: How does a language model turn your words into an answer, and why can the same question give different answers?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 5 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome to Session 5. Last time, in Session 4, you saw words become numbers, and how distance between those numbers finds similar meaning. Today you see what a language model does with numbers like those to produce an answer. I use a real open model, GPT-2, running on this laptop, so every figure on the slides is a recorded result.

You will have computed a softmax and a small self-attention yourself, with three numbers. And you will be able to explain two things clients ask: why the same question gives different answers, and why a confident answer can be wrong.

title.text:
Your two hours: most of
the time is your own work

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_d74fedb3.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: You watch a real open model work, then compute its core step with a pencil.

slides.notes:
To get there we have two hours, and most of it is your own work. We spend the first half hour on the ideas: tokens, next-token prediction like your phone keyboard, softmax and temperature, how the model is trained, self-attention explained with a classroom, and a peek inside a transformer block.

Every picture uses numbers from a real open model that I ran on a laptop. Then I run the model live, so you see tokens and probabilities appear. After the break you work a softmax by hand on paper. We end by deciding where this behaviour helps and where it hurts in your own work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is an embedding?
2.  Name two ways to measure how close two embeddings are.
3.  Why could the search find the formal contract term from a plain description?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png
objects.alt: Three questions

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 4. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is an embedding? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. A list of numbers that places a word or sentence as a point, so that similar meanings sit close together.

Question two. Name two ways to measure how close two embeddings are. Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, dot product, or cosine similarity, which compares the angle.

Question three. Why could the search find the formal contract term from a plain description? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. Because the description and the clause sit close together as points, even when they share no words.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet or workbook page has it. Now to today.

How today connects: what we
already have and what it feeds

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_chain_11.90x4.45_b8dff084.png
objects.alt: How today connects to the sessions before and after it

So where does today sit in the story? The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14, and the gold one is today.

We already hold the training loop from Session 0, neurons and layers from Session 1 and embeddings: words as numbers from Session 4. Nothing today starts from zero.

What today adds is this: next-token prediction, softmax, self-attention.

And it feeds straight into what comes next. Session 6: what happens when this is done at huge scale. Keep that chain in mind, because each idea you learn today is a step on it.

slides.notes:
6 words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Token, tokenizer. A token is a piece of text the model reads. The tokenizer cuts text into tokens from a fixed vocabulary.

Next-token prediction. The model gives a score (logit) to every token; softmax turns the logits into probabilities.

Temperature, top-k, top-p. Settings for sampling: how the next token is drawn from the probabilities.

Self-attention. Each token weighs the earlier tokens by relevance, using a query, a key and a value.

Transformer block. Self-attention followed by a feed-forward network. GPT-2 small stacks 12.

Embedding matrix. A lookup table with one row of numbers per token. Positional encoding adds position.

Keep those words close. The first idea uses them straight away, so let us begin.

title.text:
Ask the same model the same question
twice and the answers can differ

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_two_runs_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Ask the same model the same question twice and the answers can differ

objects.text: Two real runs of GPT-2, an open model, with the same words in.

slides.notes:
Here is the first idea, and it starts with a puzzle every executive has noticed. You ask an assistant the same question twice and get two different answers. I gave an open model, GPT-2, the same eight words twice. One run says the delivery was delayed. The other says it was fast and the service was excellent.

Nobody changed anything. It is not a fault. It is how the machine is built, and by the end you can explain it to a colleague and say what it means for checking answers. Where do we start? With what the machine actually reads.

title.text:
A tokenizer cuts text into tokens:
words, parts of words or punctuation

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_tokens_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A tokenizer cuts text into tokens: words, parts of words or punctuation

objects.text: A token is a piece of text the model reads. The tokenizer is the program that cuts text into tokens.

runs.text: Common words are one token.
Names, numbers and rare words split into several.
The vocabulary is the fixed list of all tokens: 50,257 in GPT-2.

slides.notes:
So what does the machine actually read?

Neither letters nor whole sentences. It reads tokens. A token is a piece of text, and the tokenizer is the program that cuts text into tokens. As an analogy, think of syllables in a word, though tokens are chosen by statistics and do not follow syllables. Common words such as flour or delivers are one token.

A name like Mbale becomes Mb and ale. An invoice number and an amount in shillings break into many small tokens. The fixed list of all tokens is the vocabulary, and each token has an id number. These are real tokens from the GPT-2 tokenizer. Does the number of tokens matter for your work?

title.text:
Amounts, names and Swahili need
more tokens than plain English

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_token_counts_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Amounts, names and Swahili need more tokens than plain English

objects.text: Real GPT-2 token counts. A second tool, tiktoken, gave the same tokens.

slides.notes:
It matters, and here is the evidence. Five NVF sentences, counted two ways. The grey bar is words. The gold bar is tokens. The invoice sentence has seven words but eighteen tokens, because the amount and the invoice number split into small tokens. The Swahili order has five words and fourteen tokens.

This matters in two ways. Providers set prices and limits in tokens, and the context window, the most tokens a model can read at once, is also counted in tokens. And a model handles rare tokens less well, because it saw them less in training.

title.text:
Next-token prediction works like phone
autocomplete, repeated again and again

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_next_loop_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Next-token prediction works like phone autocomplete, repeated again and again

objects.text: Your keyboard suggests three words. A language model scores every token, picks one, adds it and repeats.

runs.text: The raw scores are called logits.
The longer text goes back in for the next token.

slides.notes:
Once the text is in tokens, what does the model do with them?

One thing only, and you already know a small version of it. Your phone keyboard suggests the next word as you type, and you tap one. On the left are the three most likely next tokens that GPT-2 gave after Thank you for your: support at thirty percent, continued at ten and patience at five.

A real keyboard uses its own method, so read this as the same idea. A language model does next-token prediction. It gives a score, called a logit, to every token in its vocabulary, 50,257 for GPT-2. One token is picked, for example support. That token joins the text, and the longer text goes round again.

The loop has no step that looks anything up. Those logits are awkward numbers, so how do we turn them into percentages?

title.text:
Softmax turns logits into probabilities
that add up to 100 percent

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_softmax_hand_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Softmax turns logits into probabilities that add up to 100 percent

objects.text: Logits 2, 1 and 0 become 67, 24 and 9 percent.

runs.text: Formula in words: probability = 2.72 to the logit, divided by the total of all of them.
The 2.72 is the number e, rounded.
Industry name: softmax.

slides.notes:
Here is the answer. Think of a vote where bigger scores earn far bigger shares of the vote. That is an analogy for the recipe. The recipe is called softmax, and it has two steps. Raise two point seven two, which is the number e rounded, to the power of each logit.

Then divide each result by the total. With logits two, one and zero you get seven point three nine, two point seven two and one. The total is eleven point one one. Divide, and you get sixty-seven, twenty-four and nine percent. These probabilities are a probability distribution: they add up to one hundred percent.

In industry notation the recipe reads p sub i equals e to the z sub i, divided by the sum over j of e to the z sub j, where z is the logit. You do exactly this in the hands-on.

title.text:
A real probability distribution: its
shape shows how sure the model is

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_next_three_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A real probability distribution: its shape shows how sure the model is

objects.text: Real GPT-2 distributions. A tall bar is a safe prediction. Many short bars spread the bets.

slides.notes:
Now three real distributions from GPT-2, each over fifty thousand tokens, top six shown. After please pay the invoice within thirty, the model puts sixty-nine percent on an opening bracket and eighteen on days. Few good choices. After the customer was angry because the delivery was, the choices are many and close: delayed, not, late.

After Nile Valley Foods is a food distributor based in, the model has no idea and spreads its bets across American places. The real answer, Jinja, is not on the list, yet a fluent sentence still comes out. The probabilities describe likely text, not truth, and nothing in the loop checks facts.

title.text:
Temperature divides the logits before
softmax: low sharpens, high flattens

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_temp_bars_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Temperature divides the logits before softmax: low sharpens, high flattens

objects.text: Real GPT-2 logits divided by the temperature T, then softmax.

slides.notes:
A setting changes how the choice is made, and it is called temperature. Before softmax, the model divides every logit by the temperature T. At zero point two, the favourite, delayed, takes seventy-eight percent and the rest nearly vanish. At one, the probabilities are as trained: delayed has eleven percent and sixty-seven percent sits outside the top five.

At one point eight the distribution flattens, and ninety-six percent sits outside the top five, in a long tail of strange tokens. The formula is softmax with z divided by T inside the exponent: p sub i equals e to z sub i over T, over the sum of the same.

Low temperature gives repeatable answers. High temperature gives variety and eventually nonsense.

title.text:
Sampling draws one token by chance, so
low temperature repeats and high drifts

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_temp_samples_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Sampling draws one token by chance, so low temperature repeats and high drifts

objects.text: Real sampled completions, three of six per setting. Greedy decoding would always take the top token.

slides.notes:
Percentages are abstract until you read what comes out. Sampling means drawing the next token at random, in proportion to its probability. Greedy decoding is the opposite: always take the top token. I sampled completions from the same prompt at three temperatures. At zero point two, the three runs start the same way, with delayed, and one even repeats itself.

At one, the runs go in different directions: a delay, a legal requirement, a rent dispute. At one point eight the text is mostly noise. This is why the same question gives different answers. Which setting would you want for a contract summary, and which for naming products?

title.text:
Top-k and top-p cut the list before
sampling; greedy takes only the top token

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_sampling_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Top-k and top-p cut the list before sampling; greedy takes only the top token

objects.text: Top-k and top-p applied to the recorded GPT-2 distribution for "Please pay the invoice within thirty".

slides.notes:
Temperature is not the only setting. Greedy decoding keeps one token, the top one. Top-k keeps the k most probable tokens, here k equals two, so an opening bracket and days. Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, keeps the smallest group of top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p.

With p of zero point nine, the running total passes ninety percent at the third token, so three are kept. After the cut, each kept probability is divided by the total of the kept ones, so they add up to one hundred percent again, and one token is drawn at random.

Top-k with k of two gives eighty and twenty percent. I applied these filters myself to the recorded list, to remove the long tail of strange tokens.

title.text:
Training uses the Session 0 loop on text:
predict the next token, measure the loss, adjust

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_learn_loop_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Training uses the Session 0 loop on text: predict the next token, measure the loss, adjust

objects.text: Step 2 shows the trained GPT-2 for illustration. Early in training the predictions are close to random.

slides.notes:
How did the model learn to produce all this?

With the loop from Session 0: predict, measure the loss, adjust, repeat. Take a sentence from a huge body of text, here please pay the invoice within thirty, and hide the next token. The model predicts: opening bracket sixty-nine percent, days eighteen. The true token is days, so days got only eighteen percent, and the loss is high.

The loss is minus the natural log of that probability, called cross-entropy: minus ln of point one eight is about one point seven one. A perfect prediction gives zero. Over a whole text, the probability is the product of each token given the ones before it, and training lowers the average loss.

Gradient descent nudges the weights. No person wrote a label: that is self-supervised learning.

title.text:
Self-attention: in a classroom, each
pupil decides whom to listen to

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_classroom_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Self-attention: in a classroom, each pupil decides whom to listen to

objects.text: You are Esther and need a red pen. You listen most to the pupil whose key matches your query.

runs.text: Query: what a token is looking for.
Key: what a token offers, to be matched.
Value: the information it hands over.
The percentages are illustrative.

slides.notes:
Now the idea that makes modern models work, self-attention, and I start with a classroom. Imagine you are Esther and you need a red pen, so you ask a question, which is your query. Each earlier pupil holds up a card saying what they have, which is the key.

You compare your query with every key and decide how much to listen to each pupil: seventy percent to Brian, who has the red pen. Then you take what they hand over, which is the value, mostly the red pen from Brian. In the model, every token produces its own query, key and value as lists of numbers, made from its embedding by learned weights. The percentages here are illustrative.

title.text:
In a real GPT-2 attention head, "it" gives
85 percent of its attention to "invoice"

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_attn_arrows_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: In a real GPT-2 attention head, "it" gives 85 percent of its attention to "invoice"

objects.text: The sentence ends with "it". Line thickness is the attention weight.

runs.text: The weights add up to 100 percent.
A word can only look at earlier words.
This is one attention head: one set of queries, keys and values.

slides.notes:
Here is the real thing. The sentence is about a supplier, an invoice and a manager, and it ends with the word it. At that word, the model compares its query with the keys of the earlier tokens and weighs them. The thickness of each line shows the weight.

In this real attention head from GPT-2, the token it puts eighty-five percent of its attention on invoice. An attention head is one such calculation with its own query, key and value, and a block runs twelve in parallel. This head looks like it tracks what refers to what, but that is my reading of one picture. Attention is a weighting. Do not read it as understanding.

title.text: A real attention map: block 5, head 4 of GPT-2

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_attn_heat_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A real attention map: block 5, head 4 of GPT-2

objects.text: This is block 5, head 4. GPT-2 small has 12 blocks of 12 heads.

runs.text: Each row is a token looking back.
A token cannot look ahead.

slides.notes:
The same attention can be drawn as a grid, and this is the real one. Each row is the token that is looking. Each column is an earlier token it may look at. Darker red means a higher attention weight. The empty upper triangle is there because a token cannot look at tokens that come later.

The bottom row, circled, is the token it, and it puts eighty-five percent on invoice. I must be clear: this is one head of one block. GPT-2 small has twelve blocks with twelve heads each, and larger models have many more. One head shows one pattern. It does not show what the model thinks.

How typical is that tidy head?

title.text:
Most heads do something else,
and I searched for this one

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_head_grid_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Most heads do something else, and I searched for this one

objects.text: Of 144 heads, 78 put over half their attention on the first token. Only one put over 30 percent on "invoice".

runs.text: I searched all 144 to find a head that shows a clear pattern.

slides.notes:
Not very typical, and here I show the search itself. Each small square is one head, laid out by block and head number. On the left, the darker the square, the more the token it rests on the first token of the sentence. Seventy-eight of the one hundred and forty-four heads do that.

It seems to be a resting place. On the right, only one head, ringed, puts much attention on invoice. I found it by searching. So a neat attention picture is a selected example. Treat anyone who says the model attends to the right thing with caution unless they show you the search. We have the picture; now let me give it numbers.

title.text:
Self-attention by hand: score,
softmax, then blend the values

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_toy_attention_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Self-attention by hand: score, softmax, then blend the values

objects.text: Score = query x key. Weights = softmax of the scores. Output = weights x values, added up.

slides.notes:
Let me do self-attention with a pencil, with one number per query, key and value. The token it has the query two. The three earlier tokens have keys zero point five, one point five and one. Score each one as query times key: one, three and two. Now softmax: raise two point seven two to each score, divide by the total, and you get attention weights of nine, sixty-seven and twenty-four percent.

Their values, the information handed over, are two, six and four. Multiply each weight by its value and add up: about five point two, close to the value of invoice. The formula is softmax of Q times K transposed over root d k, times V. Our toy has one number per vector, so d k is one and scaling does nothing. A real GPT-2 head uses 64 numbers and divides by 8.

title.text:
The embedding matrix is a lookup table:
a token id picks one row of 768 numbers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_lookup_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The embedding matrix is a lookup table: a token id picks one row of 768 numbers

objects.text: Real GPT-2 sizes and real row 45,458. The other rows are illustrative.

slides.notes:
Before we open the model, one step we skipped: how a token becomes a list of numbers. Every token has an id, its place in the vocabulary. Invoice is number forty-five thousand, four hundred and fifty-eight. The model keeps a big table, the embedding matrix, with one row per token, and each row holds 768 numbers.

The id picks its row, like finding a name in a phone book, which is an analogy for the lookup. For GPT-2 that is fifty thousand, two hundred and fifty-seven rows. Nobody typed these numbers in. They are weights, learned by the same loop. Position comes from a second learned table of 1,024 rows, and the two rows are added: x sub t equals E of the token id plus P of the position.

title.text:
A transformer block is self-attention plus
a feed-forward network; GPT-2 stacks 12

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_block_peek_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A transformer block is self-attention plus a feed-forward network; GPT-2 stacks 12

objects.text: Real GPT-2 small sizes. Simplified: a real block also has layer normalisation and residual connections.

slides.notes:
Self-attention is half of the story, so let me open one transformer block of GPT-2. The numbers come in: each token is the list of 768 numbers just picked from the embedding matrix. First comes self-attention, which you just worked by hand. It blends in information from earlier tokens.

Then comes a feed-forward network, a layer of neurons of the kind you met in Session 1, only much wider: 3,072 of them. Numbers go out, still 768 per token. That is one block, with 7,087,872 weights. GPT-2 small stacks twelve blocks, each feeding the next, and then produces logits for all 50,257 tokens. I leave out the small steps named in the caption.

title.text:
Put together: tokens, embeddings, 12
transformer blocks, logits, probabilities

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_stack_7.70x4.80.png

slides.notes:
You now have every part, so here is the whole machine in one picture. The tokenizer cuts text into tokens. Each token becomes a row of numbers from the embedding matrix, the same idea as the embeddings from Session 4, plus its position. The numbers pass through twelve transformer blocks.

Out come fifty thousand logits, and softmax makes a probability distribution. Then one token is picked by sampling and the loop repeats. GPT-2 small has one hundred and twenty-four million parameters, all set by the training loop, and a context window of one thousand and twenty-four tokens. Modern assistants are larger in every way, but the loop is the same. Everything so far was recorded, so now I run it live.

Now you work the same arithmetic yourself, for twenty-five minutes, with a pencil or a spreadsheet, and I walk round. The worksheet has three logits. Raise two point seven two to each logit. A calculator helps. Add the three answers, then divide each by the total, so you get three probabilities.

Then divide the logits by two, which is a temperature of two, and repeat. Which temperature gives the safer answer, and which gives more variety?

The table shows the finished first half. For the second half, expect about fifty-five, thirty-three and twelve percent. Call me over when you have both sets. The formula is on the sheet: p equals e to z over T, divided by the sum of the same.

slides.notes:
You have done the arithmetic, so let us see what it means across the company. Here is the lesson turned into a table. Where a job needs variety, drafting a reply or naming a product, next-token prediction helps and you review. Where a job needs exact figures or exact wording, reconciling amounts or quoting a clause, it hurts, because the model produces what is likely and you must check against the source.

Summarising a CV is mixed. The output is fluent, and the model may add a detail that was never there. Use this table to decide where you let the tool draft and where you demand a source. Now apply it to your own desk.
